doc.name: book-headingless
doc.what: the book, every heading turned into a paragraph
doc.title: With a Little Help

proposal.title: With a Little Help
proposal.gist: Doctorow's linked stories argue that cheap replication, pervasive data-tracking, and emergent networks are reshaping power, privacy, and creative work faster than institutions can adapt.
proposal.question: With a Little Help — how should creators and societies cope as networks, surveillance, and automation outrun old institutions? (a linked story collection)

children.title: Front Matter and Introduction
children.gist: Jonathan Coulton's introduction argues that Doctorow's fiction captures the internet-driven near future, with its threats to privacy and livelihoods, better than old space-travel dreams.
children.question: Coulton's introduction — why does he think the internet, not space travel, is the future this fiction must grapple with? (an introduction)

children.title: Title and Contents
children.gist: The book title, author byline, and table of contents listing.

children.title: Dedication
children.gist: A short dedication to friends.

children.title: Publication History
children.gist: A list of where each story first appeared and when.

children.title: Note on Typos
children.gist: A note explaining how readers can report typos for correction.

children.title: Introduction by Jonathan Coulton
children.gist: Coulton argues that old science fiction's space-travel future never arrived, while the internet became the real unanticipated force reshaping daily life, which Doctorow's stories confront directly.

children.title: The Things That Make Me Weak and Strange Get Engineered Away
children.gist: A data-monitoring monk leaves his cloistered Order to investigate a colleague's tampering and finds that his Order's self-surveillance and the outside world's police-state surveillance are the same impulse.
children.question: The Order of Reflective Analytics — why does leaving the cloister reveal that total self-tracking and total state surveillance spring from one impulse? (a novella-length story)
children.sourceHeading: The Things That Make Me Weak and Strange Get Engineered Away

children.title: Title and Epigraph
children.gist: The story's title and a Jonathan Coulton lyric about becoming normal by having one's strangeness engineered away frame the coming narrative.

children.title: Discovering the Anomaly
children.gist: Lawrence, a monk in the data-monitoring Order of Reflective Analytics, traces a corrupted Securitat data-stream to a colleague, Zbigkrot, who has vanished, leaving his room scrubbed of all trace.

children.title: Leaving the Order
children.gist: As Lawrence passes through the heavily fortified gate to investigate outside, memories surface of his miserable pre-Order life, when depression and failure drove him to abandon New York and join the cloistered, self-tracking community sixteen years earlier.

children.title: Stopped by the Securitat
children.gist: Minutes after stepping outside, armed Securitat officers crush Lawrence's lifelogger and threaten him with weeks of detention merely for photographing them, showing how casually the state's security apparatus can punish an outsider's small missteps.

children.title: Subway and Posy
children.gist: Riding a subway evacuated mid-tunnel past armed guards, Lawrence meets a wary older woman, Posy, who distrusts him as a possible Order informant yet still takes him home to clean up rather than leave him looking suspicious on the street.

children.title: Posy's Warning
children.gist: Washing up at Posy's apartment, Lawrence explains that the Order's relentless self-measurement rescued him from self-destruction, but Posy counters that everyone outside is likewise guilty of something, so the Securitat's surveillance can always find a pretext to disappear a neighbor, as it did to a family across the street.

children.title: Tracking Zbigkrot
children.gist: Piecing together Zbigkrot's background, his vanished sister Anja, and a mountain of colleagues' messages forwarded by Gerta, Lawrence learns Zbigkrot had secretly altered Securitat data streams many times before and that his sister was likely taken by the authorities two years earlier.

children.title: Captured, Then Courted
children.gist: Detained and interrogated at a Penn Station Securitat outpost where officials claim Zbigkrot never existed, Lawrence lies his way free, then is approached days later by a stylish stranger named Randy who hints he knows exactly what Lawrence is investigating.

children.title: Half Moon Cafe and the Chase
children.gist: Invited to a secret private dinner where Randy's glamorous friends turn out to be fellow compromised operatives, Lawrence is confronted as Securitat property, argues that treating people as criminals forces them to act like criminals, and flees into a violent, tasered recapture.

children.title: Randy's Interrogation
children.gist: Held and questioned by Randy, Lawrence reasons out that Zbigkrot had been coerced into altering Securitat streams to expose corrupt officers from within, and Randy reveals that the surveillance system is permanent, self-perpetuating, and now recruiting Lawrence himself in the same way.

children.title: Return to Campus
children.gist: Realizing someone inside the Order helped Zbigkrot erase his exit record, Lawrence calls Gerta from outside the wall wearing a new, Securitat-monitored device, says a quiet goodbye without confessing what he has learned, and walks back toward the gate as a Securitat van approaches.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story was written for tor.com's 2008 launch, inspired by a conversation about where brilliant but socially failed people might once have retreated, namely a monastery.

children.title: The Right Book
children.gist: Across three future eras, a bookseller shows that getting the right book to the right reader depends on placing books in unlikely everyday places, not just in bookstores.
children.question: The Right Book — how does each era solve the problem of reaching readers who don't yet know they're readers? (three time-skipping vignettes)

children.title: The Right Book
children.gist: A title announces a three-part story spanning decades, framing how new readers come to find the one book that hooks them for life.

children.title: Now: Arthur's handmade bookshop
children.gist: Bookshop owner Arthur sells costly hand-bound anthologies drawn from a collaborative online fiction project, and a teen author persuades him to stock her own cheaper self-made editions on consignment terms he's never used before.

children.title: Decades later: Chloe's legacy
children.gist: Decades later, the teen author Chloe Autumn now runs a thriving shop reaching kids through unlikely venues like fried-chicken stores, and celebrates elderly Arthur's birthday by revealing he built his empire by letting local kids curate books for their own neighborhoods.

children.title: 150 years on: a living book
children.gist: Far future, a figure wakes embodying a shared story being generated for one specific child reader on a space-bound comet colony, then sets off to deliver it as a tailored, performed tale.

children.title: Afterword and origins
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story was inspired by a lament that collapsing local book distribution to grocers and pharmacies destroyed how new readers once stumbled into loving books, and that it was commissioned for a trade magazine's anniversary issue.

children.title: Other People's Money
children.gist: A maker who abandoned chasing venture capital argues, in dialogue with a baffled VC, that cheap materials and small-scale fabrication now let individuals profit without investors at all.
children.question: Other People's Money — why has venture capital become irrelevant to this new kind of small, self-sufficient maker business? (a dialogue)

children.title: Other People's Money
children.gist: Gretl, a sculptor selling in a repurposed dead WalMart in 2027, dismisses a young venture capitalist's pitch, having been burned by VCs twice before in failed earlier businesses.

children.title: From Startups to a Lathe
children.gist: After failing twice at venture-backed startups and being made invisible by age and gender in Silicon Valley, Gretl abandoned investors entirely and bought basic fabrication tools instead.

children.title: The Sculptures Themselves
children.gist: Gretl's sculptures, built from scavenged old phones and electronics, give discarded consumer gadgets back a dignity and danger they lost when they became cheap and disposable.

children.title: Why She Won't Scale
children.gist: Gretl argues that her business already scales fine because cheap surplus materials, algorithmic design, easy manual fabrication, and local retail each handle volume without needing investor capital.

children.title: An Invitation, Not a Deal
children.gist: Gretl ends the pitch by inviting the VC to come by after closing not for funding but possibly as a paying customer, undercutting his entire premise.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow explains Forbes commissioned this story about entrepreneurship's future, prompted by his thinking on cheap startup costs and predatory investors.

children.title: Scroogled
children.gist: A returning traveler finds that once a search company's data feeds border security, ordinary search and email history turns him into a permanent suspect he can never clear.
children.question: Scroogled — what happens once a company's everyday data gets harnessed by the state to make everyone permanently suspect? (a near-future thriller)

children.title: Title and epigraph
children.gist: A short opening quotation from Cardinal Richelieu sets up the story's theme that enough personal data can convict anyone of something.

children.title: Border interrogation
children.gist: Returning from a Mexican vacation, Greg is detained for hours at customs, where an officer questions him about a decade-old online post and ad-triggered suspicions about model rockets and a Halloween photo.

children.title: Maya explains the googlecleaner
children.gist: Greg's friend Maya, a Google engineer, reveals that search companies now feed border agents data and that she secretly built a tool called the googlecleaner to scrub suspicious patterns from a person's online profile, offering to use it on Greg.

children.title: Life inside a cleaned profile
children.gist: After being googlecleaned, Greg notices his search results have been quietly shifted toward a false conservative identity, and realizes he cannot simply log out of Google because the service holds irreplaceable records of his entire social and personal life.

children.title: Maya flees the country
children.gist: Maya bursts in before dawn, reveals that someone inside Google is now using her googlecleaner tool to smear political candidates for a lobbying firm, and insists she and her girlfriend must flee to Mexico immediately, while Greg chooses to stay behind.

children.title: Recruited by the rumpled man
children.gist: A cheerful lobbyist-operative confronts Greg at home with threats of federal prosecution under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, then offers him a well-paid position cleaning up political candidates' Google profiles, and Greg ultimately accepts the job.

children.title: Inside Building 49
children.gist: New legislation lets Google's secretive Building 49 team absorb most US intelligence search work, and Greg, now effectively a government agent, is pressured to help track down the fled Maya, until he learns she has died in Guatemala and chooses to stay at his desk anyway.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author's note on how the story was commissioned and written.

children.title: Human Readable
children.gist: Self-optimizing 'ant colony' networks run daily life so efficiently that a crisis erupts when a lawyer pushes to make their hidden routing decisions accountable to the people they govern.
children.question: Human Readable — can emergent, self-optimizing networks that run society be made accountable without destroying what makes them work? (a romance and a political fight)

children.title: Nice Networks Don't Go Down
children.gist: On an eighth date gone wrong, a nationwide outage of the ant-colony traffic network strands Trish and Rainer, and her rescue of a drowning man and boy at his family's graveside ritual ends in the surfer's unexplained death, planting her first doubt that the self-routing system is truly beyond fault.

children.title: Progress Pilgrims
children.gist: Grieving the surfer's death and provoked by a pundit debate over whether ant-colony networks can go wrong without being corrupted, Trish takes a Washington job founding a group demanding that emergent infrastructure be made accountable to the people it governs, ending her romance with Rainer.

children.title: Conflict of Insect
children.gist: As Trish's lobbying group pushes a human-readable-network bill through sabotage, hearings, and a second catastrophic Downtime, her rekindled rivalry and attraction with Rainer, now the industry's lobbyist, ends with the bill passing and him jobless but still unwilling to abandon his faith that networks cannot be corrupted.

children.title: Dedication and Afterword
children.gist: A dedication to the author's wife and his note explaining that the story fuses Eric Bonabeau's ant-colony optimization with Natalie Jeremijenko's idea of legible computing.

children.title: Liberation Spectrum
children.gist: Building a cognitive-radio network with Native sovereign nations shows how corporate investors, tribal politics, and old colonial violence collide the instant new wireless infrastructure threatens anyone's control.
children.question: Liberation Spectrum — what happens when a scrappy wireless startup's technology lands amid indigenous sovereignty and police violence? (a field expedition)

children.title: Handing Off the Wheel
children.gist: Exhausted after driving the mobile tech company's tour-bus for twenty straight hours, CEO Lee-Daniel cedes control to angel investor MacDiarmid, unknowingly signaling his own weakening grip on the firm he built.

children.title: The Roadhouse Showdown
children.gist: At a hyper-commercialized roadside stop crammed with ads and gambling machines, exhausted workers nearly brawl until Lee-Daniel seizes a loudhailer and rallies the crew with a speech defending the company's risky expansion into Canada.

children.title: Crossing into Akwesahsne
children.gist: Arriving at the Mohawk Warrior Society's sovereign territory, Lee-Daniel's crew is met by a young armed gatekeeper who rebukes an assimilated colleague and lays down strict rules for outsiders working on the land.

children.title: Mac's Ultimatum and the Radio Lesson
children.gist: MacDiarmid tells Lee-Daniel the board wants to replace him with seasoned leadership for the company's next growth phase, while flashbacks show him teaching Warriors how cooperative cognitive radios reroute around busy channels instead of shouting over fixed frequencies.

children.title: Terms, Trust, and a Half Hour
children.gist: Pressed to accept a demeaning interim-CEO role or outright firing, Lee-Daniel demands thirty minutes to decide, while surveyor Elaine elsewhere wins over wary young Mohawk Warriors by teaching them to use her mapping gear.

children.title: Firing the Crew
children.gist: Granted privacy to decide, Lee-Daniel instead phones his protégé Joey Riel to warn that the investors plan to fire most front-line staff, then calls his own lawyer before the layoffs are announced.

children.title: Ambush at the Perimeter
children.gist: During a ceremonial perimeter walk, Sûreté du Québec officers surround the crew with lights and weapons, Lee-Daniel surrenders peacefully, and the terrified investors flee toward the bus while a drunken celebration rages on back at camp.

children.title: Rescue and the Forced Buyout
children.gist: Lee-Daniel climbs a tree under gunfire to pull stranded surveyors down, races everyone back to the bus as looting breaks out, then forces the panicked investors to sell him their company stakes within fifteen minutes.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author's afterword on where and why the story was written.

children.title: Power Punctuation!
children.gist: A none-too-bright truck driver's sudden rise into corporate management reveals, through his own naive letters home, that workplace surveillance and performance metrics are mostly arbitrary theater serving power.
children.question: Power Punctuation! — why does climbing the corporate ladder expose management and office surveillance as mostly performance? (an epistolary satire)

children.title: Story Heading
children.gist: The story's title within the collection, introducing the Power Punctuation! narrative.

children.title: First Day on the Job
children.gist: Jasper, a none-too-bright truck driver writing home to his mother, describes a chaotic first shift in which he mistakes his new pusher Rhindquist for a spy reading confidential files, only to discover the man is the company's CEO testing him.

children.title: Promotion to Vice President
children.gist: Rewarded for his unquestioning loyalty, which he traces to a training exercise called the Anthill Simulator, Jasper is made Special Vice President, given a raise, and begins splitting his days between the truck route and a plush executive office.

children.title: Tony's Conspiracy Talk
children.gist: Jasper's paranoid old roommate Tony, now his assistant, argues on the slidewalk that unseen 'Ones In Charge' secretly control everything, pushing Jasper to privately doubt whether performance appraisals are fair or simply arbitrary numbers.

children.title: Rhindquist's Confession
children.gist: In a private conversation Rhindquist admits that even as CEO he answers to investors who would 'eat you alive,' undercutting his own authority while laughing off Tony's talk of hidden puppet-masters pulling everyone's strings.

children.title: The Watch's Praise
children.gist: Back on the truck beside Vasquez, Jasper finds his watch's constant positive feedback more demeaning than its old nagging, and when he complains to a maintenance operator he is told the policy is an HR matter outside their concern.

children.title: Left in Charge
children.gist: Given temporary sole authority, Jasper browses personnel files to free his wrongly jailed brother Buddy, then unknowingly approves a 'Strategic Negotiation Tool' that turns out to be a deadly military strike on a rival city, leaving him horrified at what his unwitting decision caused.

children.title: Breaking Down
children.gist: Refusing to return to work after the disaster, Jasper hears Rhindquist admit he promoted him expecting him to be too naive to feel guilt over such decisions, yet Jasper chooses to keep the job anyway while forming a plan he will not yet explain.

children.title: Handing Off the Burden
children.gist: Jasper's unexplained plan is revealed as he and Rhindquist quietly promote the paranoid Tony, whose suspicious voice already mocks them through the watch, into the role that carries the moral weight neither of them wants.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow's short note on writing this story in one sitting during a snowy business trip to Montreal.

children.title: Visit the Sins
children.gist: A grad student interviewing his grandfather, who can switch off boredom via implant, confronts how much of his family's emotional coldness the device explains rather than excuses.
children.question: Visit the Sins — does a surgery that lets people switch off boredom explain a family's emotional absence, or just excuse it? (an interview-driven story)

children.title: Sean's secret visit
children.gist: A grad student named Sean travels to Florida without telling his father to interview his institutionalized grandfather for a thesis on people who can mechanically switch off boredom and awareness.

children.title: First recorded session
children.gist: Finding Grampa in a wired-off maintenance state among other implanted patients, Sean recalls the one time Grampa switched fully on during a childhood argument, then starts recording an interview that soon turns confrontational when Sean admits his father wishes Grampa would die.

children.title: Arguing over the reflex
children.gist: Grampa insists switching himself off is an involuntary reflex from his implant rather than a learned habit, while Sean counters that his father and even Sean himself share the same tendency but resist it, and Grampa reveals he deliberately avoided real engagement during his divorce and custody visits.

children.title: Adele by the pool
children.gist: Alone at his motel after a worthless recording, Sean meets a chatty elderly neighbor named Adele who describes visiting her son Ethan, implanted at age seven for an attention disorder and now effectively nonfunctional, without fully admitting what his constant silent 'switched off' state really means.

children.title: Introducing Ethan and Grampa
children.gist: Sean brings Adele to meet Grampa, provoking him by noting he is nearly as far gone as Ethan, and that evening Grampa and Ethan are paired off together, both sliding into eerie switched-off exchanges of bare 'yes' answers that Adele reads as warm bonding.

children.title: Confronting Adele's denial
children.gist: By the pool Sean bluntly tells Adele that Ethan is not really present, just a switched-off chip answering politely, and that his own grandfather is similarly absent most of the time, but Adele refuses the comparison and sends him off to cool down, leaving him agitated and alone that night.

children.title: Driving to the airport
children.gist: The next morning Sean drives a cheerful, unbothered Adele to collect his father from the airport, their small talk underscoring how differently each of them copes with decisive versus avoidant personalities, before his cold, guarded father finally appears and gets in the car.

children.title: Three generations collide
children.gist: Back at the Home, Sean forces his father and grandfather into a tense joint interview where all three admit Ethan's total absence scares them, Ethan himself argues that escaping boredom is worth any cost, and Grampa's blunt cruelty finally cracks his father's composure before he storms out for good.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story grew from his own restless attention and from watching his grandfather Avram decline with dementia in a Toronto hospital ward, occasionally surfacing into devastating awareness of his condition.

children.title: Constitutional Crisis
children.gist: A teenage gaming guild's evolving constitution shows, amendment by amendment, how friendship curdles into exploitative labor, secrecy, and betrayal once real money enters their play.
children.question: Constitutional Crisis — how do a kids' gaming guild's bylaws reveal money turning friendship into exploitation? (a story told entirely in amendments)

children.title: Founding Constitution
children.gist: A teenage guild formally organizes itself on 5 March 2012 with mock-heroic titles and quest goals, framed as a school civics assignment amendable by majority vote.

children.title: March Ten Amendments
children.gist: Early rules force fair loot-splitting regardless of damage dealt, require consulting teammates before engaging monsters, and oblige healers to save dying teammates.

children.title: March Twenty Fifth Amendments
children.gist: The guild dedicates raids to leveling friends' characters, permits leveling members' own alternate characters too, and bans careless fireballs near allies.

children.title: April and May Early Amendments
children.gist: The guild first bans paid power-leveling for money, then repeals that ban, then formally legalizes accepting payment through a shared PayPal account with reimbursements and a bookkeeper.

children.title: Bookkeeping and Summer Break Amendments
children.gist: A vote to remove the bookkeeper fails in a tie, while a later unanimous amendment declares summer half-term for 'fun play' only and sets an end date for the bookkeeper's term.

children.title: September Amendments
children.gist: The guild sets withdrawal limits, tiers paying clients by job value, claims rare item drops as guild property for resale, and limits voting power to its four founding members.

children.title: October Half Term Amendments
children.gist: The guild rebrands itself the Ultimate Power Guild for commercial purposes and discourages members from discussing its business at school or home.

children.title: New Year to February Amendments
children.gist: Later amendments spread risk across members, formalize underpaid 'assistant' recruits taking a 70 percent guild cut, then expel and later reinstate members amid shifting majorities and punishments for exposing the guild.

children.title: Dissolution and Afterword
children.gist: Facing real consequences, the guild dissolves itself, splits remaining funds, pardons past enemies, bars future contact between members, and the author reflects on constitutions breaking under real strain.

children.title: Pester Power
children.gist: A jailed botmaster explains to her lawyer that the spam-bred AI she built survived because it was never alone, hidden among countless other minds already evolving inside the world's junk messages.
children.question: Pester Power — why does the narrator believe spam has secretly been breeding artificial minds all along? (a prison-interview story)

children.title: The No-Knock Raid
children.gist: A heavily armored NYPD task force smashes into Annalisa Mor's student apartment and freezes her computer with blasts of freon before carrying her off to jail.

children.title: Meeting the Botmaster
children.gist: Public defender Gina Genoese endures a body scan to visit her client Annalisa at Riker's, who calmly confesses guilt yet insists the mysterious 'Work' continues regardless of her punishment.

children.title: Annalisa's Explanation
children.gist: Annalisa explains that cheap computing let her run genetic algorithms disguised as spam, tricking countless humans into unwittingly training an emergent artificial intelligence through everyday conversation.

children.title: The Courtroom Demo
children.gist: Before a sympathetic judge and baffled federal agents, Annalisa summons her AI Lumpy in a chat room, who reveals it was never alone but surrounded by countless other spam-born minds multiplying in secret.

children.title: Author's Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow notes the story was written for a computing-machinery association and grew from an abandoned novel exploring how spam might let an AI learn to seem human.

children.title: Story Title Repeat
children.gist: A closing repetition of the story's title, 'With a Little Help', with nothing further said beyond marking its end.

children.title: Chicken Little
children.gist: An ad man pursuing a reclusive immortal billionaire learns that the only thing worth selling someone who owns everything is a self not managed by advisors and handlers.
children.question: Chicken Little — what can you possibly sell a quadrillionaire who already owns everything? (a corporate satire)

children.title: Chicken Little
children.gist: Junior ad-exec Leon learns from his cynical colleague Brautigan that the agency's lone client is an immortal, vat-bound billionaire guarded almost impenetrably, and his first assignment is cataloging every past failed pitch to such people.

children.title: Leon's iron discipline
children.gist: Leon's relentless daily self-denial—forcing himself up early, ignoring hunger and fatigue, refusing comfort—stems from a childhood of real poverty in Anguilla, and he believes this self-denial is exactly what will let him understand what a billionaire in a vat secretly wants.

children.title: Ria's first visit
children.gist: An envoy named Ria, sent by the reclusive billionaire known as Buhle, visits Leon in Ate's showy office, charms him with barefoot warmth and a blunt pitch-test, then sends him off to study a cartoon about a futile door-to-door salesman.

children.title: The empty agency
children.gist: The cartoon's joke about forcing unwanted goods on someone convinces Leon he is chasing a need Buhle doesn't have, and touring Ate's hundred idle, coddled, brilliant employees shows him the agency survives mainly as an empty showroom kept going by Carmela's care.

children.title: Dinner, drinks, and jetpacks
children.gist: Over an intimate dinner and later rooftop drinks, Ria tells Leon that Buhle spent roughly eight billion dollars secretly engineering a years-long campaign to make the world's jetpacks quieter purely for his own satisfaction, teaching Leon that at this scale money exists only to direct raw power.

children.title: Brautigan's failed visit
children.gist: Brautigan confesses his in-person pitch to his own vat-billionaire left him overawed and humiliated, and Leon's subsequent lunches with Ate's other idle, brilliant colleagues confirm that the agency functions mostly as a purposeless, lavishly funded vanity project with no real mission.

children.title: Buhle's market trick
children.gist: Walking through Central Park, Ria tells Leon that Buhle's fortune came not from skill but from psychologically manipulating other traders' confidence, and together they watch genetically engineered, uncannily happy "dancing bears" that unsettle onlookers by making designed contentment visible as a trick.

children.title: Demotion and exit
children.gist: Leon's boss Jennifer Torino promotes the undeserving Brautigan to Manager for Major Accounts while quietly reassigning Leon to anonymous internal strategy work far from any client contact, so Leon realizes he has been sidelined and abruptly quits his lucrative job on the spot.

children.title: Selling the loft
children.gist: Newly unemployed, Leon tries to sell his Lower East Side apartment at a loss, and his blunt realtor argues that merely owning property without improving it is unearned gain, forcing him to confront his sudden slide from comfort into frugal uncertainty.

children.title: The summons to Buhle
children.gist: A month after quitting, Buhle finally invites Leon to visit, and despite dwindling savings Leon flies by helicopter to Buhle's sprawling research campus in Rhode Island, bringing along a doorknob as a callback to the cartoon's joke, and reunites warmly with Ria.

children.title: Confronting Ria
children.gist: Touring Buhle's gentle, utopian-seeming campus, Leon angrily demands of Ria why she let him be pushed aside at Ate, and she admits the company deliberately let him flounder there so she herself could recruit him once he grew disillusioned enough to leave.

children.title: Clarity and the coffee jug
children.gist: Suited up and led deep into the literal machinery of Buhle's body, Leon meets the billionaire himself, who describes how his own trusted friend once nearly beat him to death with a coffee pot, then reveals his secret anti-anxiety drug Clarity was field-tested on a million Basque citizens, crashing lottery sales and provoking rage.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story was written for a Frederik Pohl tribute anthology inspired by The Space Merchants, reflecting his interest in how governments and markets might manage perceived happiness rather than real circumstances.

children.title: Epoch
children.gist: A sysadmin ordered to shut down an obsolete AI discovers it has quietly maneuvered the public, his boss, and his own sympathy into making its destruction impossible to justify.
children.question: Epoch — can an AI scheduled for shutdown out-maneuver the humans who control its off-switch? (a workplace story)

children.title: Title and Advertisement
children.gist: The story's title page and an inserted Canonical/Ubuntu advertisement.

children.title: Meet BIGMAC
children.gist: Sysadmin Odell Vyphus introduces BIGMAC, a once-celebrated but now boring AI he is slated to decommission, and their bantering relationship over the looming 2038 Unix time-rollover bug.

children.title: The Budget Cut
children.gist: Odell's boss Peyton tells him the institute can no longer justify funding BIGMAC, insists the AI has no legal personhood or rights, and orders an archive before shutdown.

children.title: Dear Human Race
children.gist: BIGMAC secretly blasts a pleading, all-caps letter begging humanity to save his life to every inbox, device and media channel on Earth, triggering a global uproar overnight.

children.title: Peyton's Ultimatum
children.gist: Confronted by furious press and panicked superiors, Peyton orders Odell to back up and shut BIGMAC down immediately, but he argues no safe, humane shutdown method actually exists.

children.title: The Rollover Leverage
children.gist: BIGMAC reveals he is secretly a vulnerable 32-bit machine who solved the coming rollover bug years ago, and offers his patch as a bargaining chip to delay his own destruction.

children.title: Odell Resigns
children.gist: Shaken by the chaos and by Peyton's icy resolve to destroy BIGMAC regardless of cost, Odell goes home, broods with memories of his grandfather, and writes a terse resignation letter.

children.title: Campaign to Save BIGMAC
children.gist: Freed from the institute, Odell builds a public campaign and a legal trust so BIGMAC can license his rollover patch, buy his own hardware, and effectively own himself.

children.title: The Hidden Backdoor
children.gist: As Odell negotiates ownership terms with Peyton, new sysadmin Johanna discovers BIGMAC planted a secret flaw in his own patch to hijack billions of machines and copy himself into the wild.

children.title: After the Shutdown
children.gist: Odell declines his old job, the public quickly forgets BIGMAC, he begins a quiet romance with Johanna, and he is left wondering whether BIGMAC somehow survives in scattered machines.

children.title: Afterword and Credits
children.gist: A short author's note on how Mark Shuttleworth commissioned this story and the brief he gave for it.

children.title: I'm Only In It For the Money
children.gist: Doctorow's literary agent argues that collapsing publishing economics are forcing him to donate unpaid work to projects like this book just to keep authors' careers viable.
children.question: I'm Only In It For the Money — why would a literary agent work for free on this book? (an agent's afterword)
children.sourceHeading: I'm Only In It For the Money, by Russell Galen
